notice: Who was Hermia the Wayfarer? “Far-ranging Hermia, fleet of foot but equally quick to take offense. She boasted that no land could escape her tread, and thus sought out Pakilykos, condemned by the wind and waves to the ocean’s floor.” How do you know Aerekostes? “Long have I known the blade, yet longer have I known the one who inhabits it. We met when they were still coming into their power. I gave them counsel until the Sky Father saw fit to take my hearing. The sword’s story is theirs to tell, but you will not find a better tutor of hero-gods in all of Iblydos.” Can you tell us the tale of Pakilykos? “Wealthy was the port of Pakilykos, prosperous centuries ago in both trade and peace. Feared Exthenios, vile pirate and lauded butcher, sought to sack the island of its wealth. Red-stained streets were his undoing, his crew cursed to shed strong muscle and barred from the Underworld—ill fate shared by any seeking to steal from Pakilykan soil. Drawn to the seabed is tragic Pakilykos, awaiting the song of Gozreh’s lyre.” The sound of a lyre can raise the island? “Only an instrument of the wind and waves, its frame carved from a leviathan whose claws touch the sky, and strung with hair of merfolk born on windswept land.” Katlanthe frowns sorrowfully, a pang of regret crossing her face. “Fabled instrument of my possession was lent to Aerekostes more than a decade past. Now lost on wretched Pakilykos.” Katlanthe informs the PCs that a replacement lyre can be crafted, but doing so requires a claw taken from one of Gozreh’s mightiest sea creatures for its frame, and hair from a merfolk born on land for the strings. She confirms that the blank spot on Captain Yasmenei's map is the hunting ground of one of Gozreh’s favored beasts and that the location marked with the image of the fish-tailed woman is home to a group of merfolk blessed by Gozreh for the paeans they offer to the winds. She can also show the PCs the location of Pakilykos before the island sank into the sea. The now-empty expanse is a full week’s voyage from Katlanthe’s island, though luckily the PCs’ current route takes them in that general direction. Treasure: If the PCs indicate they plan to reconstruct Gozreh’s lyre, Katlanthe blesses the endeavor. She motions to a member of the chorus, who steps forward and gifts the party a box made of driftwood. The box holds two marvelous miniatures (boat) and a corked glass bottle containing bottled air. Non-merfolk creatures in a 120-foot emanation must attempt a DC 25 Will save or become confused for 1 round. The creature can’t target merfolk while confused in this way. If the merfolk uses this ability again on subsequent rounds, they extend the duration by 1 round for all affected creatures. Once a creature succeeds at any save against Storm Song, that creature is temporarily immune to Storm Song for 24 hours. Development: If the merfolk are made helpful, they willingly part with enough hair to string a lyre. The merfolk also share what they know about the recent events in Iblydos. Notably, they inform the party that they’ve sensed magical energies on the winds and, in recent weeks, have even spotted strange humanoid shapes rising from the sea foam around their isle. Though the merfolk don’t know the origin of these phenomena, they are a result of Sangeh stirring, as the titan reflexively rewrites reality with her artistry. Finally, the merfolk can fill in some of the details regarding what the PCs know about Pakilykos. The merfolk claim the island was dragged beneath the sea after its people turned away from Gozreh in favor of Chinostes, the hero-god worshipped by their ruler, King Herrion. Though the sounds of the lyre might rise Pakilykos from the sea temporarily, the PCs must appease Gozreh to keep the island in place above the waves. If the PCs show them a map of the surrounding sea, the merfolk confirm that Pakilykos was once located in the area indicated by Katlanthe. If the PCs kill the merfolk, they can still retrieve their hair (though they’ll need to wash out the blood before using the hair to string the lyre). Reward: Award the PCs 120 XP if they successfully negotiate with the merfolk. Cursed Pakilykos Any PC trained in Crafting or Performance can use the Ketos’s claw and merfolk’s hair to construct a lyre to replace the one Katlanthe loaned Hermia. (If none of the PCs are trained in those skills, one of the crew members constructs the lyre for them.) Though the lyre by itself has no magical properties, as soon as it is finished the PCs can feel the instrument vibrate with mythic power, as if Gozreh themselves had blessed it. With their new lyre in hand, the hero-gods need only journey to the empty expanse of sea indicated by Katlanthe or the merfolk. Once there, the Tide Hunter drops anchor, and Captain Yasmenei orders the crew to busy themselves with ship tasks—and keep out of the party’s way. Katlanthe gave the PCs no special instructions as to how to play the lyre, and indeed, none are needed: a few plucks of the lyre’s strings are all it takes to rouse Pakilykos from the sea. As the final notes from the lyre fade into the distance, and uneasy silence settles on the sea. For a brief, dead moment, nothing seems to happen. Then, waves begin to churn about the Tide Hunter, causing the ship to lurch back and forth at sickening angles. With a tremendous roar, an island rises from the sea: first, the angled roof of a temple, followed by the building itself, and then the entire acropolis around it. The wall of water displaced by the island’s sudden appearance slams into the Tide Hunter, and it is only the skill of Captain Yasmenei and her crew that keeps the vessel from capsizing. When the wave passes, the Tide Hunter floats a mere hundred feet away from the city’s seawall: an enormous structure of stacked stone as solid as a castle’s curtain wall. Inside the seawall’s protective arc stretches a row of ancient-looking piers. Beyond the rotted pylons, a roadway choked with silt and seaweed stretches into the eerily silent city. TITANBANE Chapter 1: In Search of a Blade Chapter 2: Shades of PolDhuraxilis Chapter 3: A Sleeping Titan Wakes Continuing the Campaign Kardaji Bay Adventure Toolbox Captain Yasmenei makes a warding sign at the sight of the island before regaining her composure. “An isle of the dead is no place for sailors,” she says, only a slight quaver in her voice. “We’ll stay here to guard the ship, should you need a place to return and rest. Please, do not have us wait long.” Pakilykos is in supernaturally good condition after centuries on the ocean floor. The stone buildings are mostly intact, though any structures or furnishings made of wood have long since rotted away, and a layer of silt and displaced sea life covers most surfaces. Aside from the occasional sound of water draining from a rooftop or a fish flopping in the mud, the city is deathly silent. Unless otherwise noted, the interiors of most structures have 10-foot-high ceilings, with chambers illuminated by everlight crystals affixed to the walls with (now quite tarnished) bronze fittings. 11 Treasure: The inhabitants of Pakilykos preferred to invest their wealth rather than display it. Scavenging the empty dwellings turns up little of value. The buildings themselves are austere, with no gilding or finery. That said, it’s worth reviewing the PCs’ wealth to confirm that it’s roughly in line with what they’re expected to have by 7th level (GM Core 61), seeding a few additional trinkets if the PCs need a little extra spending money—especially since Chapter 2 presents the PCs last major opportunity to shop for gear. The following are several additional treasures the PCs might discover while exploring Pakilykos. • A finger-sized prism made of the soft, pale skymetal inubrix, a metal of similar density and hardness to lead but famed for its ability to pass through iron and steel. The prism has various markings along its length, indicating a ferrous object’s composition based on how far an assayer can press the prism into the object. The device is worth 40 gp. • A hematite cylinder seal—a tiny cylinder stamp designed to be rolled over wet clay or inked to mark paper—whose design displays three hunting dogs pulling down a manticore mid-air. The seal is worth 25 gp and grants a +1 item bonus to checks to Create Forgeries regarding Pakilykos. • An ivory scroll tube sealed in wax is worth 5 gp, but the real prize is held inside: a fragile, fragmentary parchment that records most of the recipe for phadgadei, a secretive way of preserving olives whose technique has been lost for generations. This could be sold for 25 gp. However, if kept, a PC could decipher the recipe and use it to Earn Income as a 9th-level Cooking Lore task. After a year of Earning Income in this way, others deduce the recipe and end the PC’s edge. Mythic Points: Using Gozreh’s lyre to raise Pakilykos from the sea is a mythic deed, restoring 3 Mythic Points to each character. Development: The seawall the PCs spot on their approach to the island is the source of many of Pakilykos’s troubles. King Herrion ordered the structure built to protect the city from the storms that plagued the island, but in doing so he unknowingly angered the city’s patron deity, Gozreh. Other than its impressive size, for now the seawall is unremarkable, but the PCs will have to destroy the structure if they want to keep the island from returning to the ocean’s floor (see Cleansing Pakilykos on page 20). Using the lyre to raise Pakilykos drains the instrument of its mythic power. However, a PC who plays the lyre while Aiding checks made to destroy the seawall gains a +2 item bonus to their Performance check. 12 A1. Customs House Moderate 7 The first building of note the PCs encounter along the roadway from the pier is a warehouse with an entrance wide enough to allow two carts to enter sideby-side. Weathered red paint on the stones leading to the entrance marks a pair of distinct lanes: one labeled “entry” and the other “exit.” The interior of the building reeks of rot, the stacks of waterlogged ledgers strewn about the tiled floor being the obvious culprit. The red lanes on the ground continue from the entrance to the west, leading to a platform elevated high enough that anyone standing atop it would receive a view well above the heads of anyone below. A plaque of tarnished bronze on the wall behind the platform reads “Customs.” When Pakilykos was still a thriving trade center, this building served as the harbor’s customs house. Captains would unload their cargo onto carts, then deliver them to the dockmaster for inspection. From atop the elevated platform, a single bureaucrat could see both the ships docked at the pier and the contents of each cart before them. At sundown, the customs house would be closed for regular business, but a handful of clerks would labor long into the night to transcribe the dockmaster’s notes and sort the ledgers accordingly. Creatures: The dockmaster at the time of Pakilykos’s fall was an exacting woman named Deianire. When Exthenios and his crew attacked, Deianire locked her clerks inside the customs house and fled to the temple of Chinostes (area C1) to summon help. Mistaking the locked building for a treasure vault, the pirates broke down the doors and rushed inside. When they found ledgers instead of gold, Exthenios ordered his subordinates to murder the clerks, sparking the killing spree that would eventually consume the entire island. Now, the spirits of the four clerks toil here, endlessly sorting the rotting ledgers as they await Deianire’s return. The poltergeists flit from one stack of ledgers to the next, all the while muttering descriptions of cargo (“Fourteen bushels grain. Six oxen.”) before howling in frustration and scattering the ledgers again. The spirits don’t acknowledge the party unless the characters address them or otherwise interfere with their work, at which point they wail in panic that Deianire will be furious if she finds the customs house in such a state. A character can help the clerks sort the ledgers by succeeding at a DC 21 Mercantile Lore or DC 23 Society check. With two successes, the customs house is arranged to the spirits’ liking, but a failed check causes them to attack. POLTERGEISTS (4) CREATURE 5 Pathfinder Monster Core 268 Initiative +11 Development: If the PCs placate the spirits, they can ask questions about the state of Pakilykos. While the poltergeists haven’t left the customs house since their deaths, they can share details about the island up to the night of the attack. Still in a state of shock and not quite registering their deaths, they urge the players to visit the depository (area A3), King Herrion’s home (area B), and the temple of Chinostes (area C), as those are the most likely places to find survivors. Treasure: Tucked beneath the dockmaster’s counter are two greater comprehension elixirs (Pathfinder Player Core 2 287). Each vial is labeled “for babblers.” Deianire kept the elixirs to communicate with visitors who didn’t speak Common, though she despised the need to do so. Reward: If the party avoids combat with the poltergeists by helping them sort the ledgers, award the characters 80 XP. A2. Barricade Severe 7 Several hundred feet up the roadway, a hastily erected barricade blocks the party’s path. Once the pirates’ killing spree began, the town guard rallied here to keep Exthenios and his crew from progressing beyond the piers. Unfortunately, the guards were more accustomed to corralling drunken sailors than bloodthirsty corsairs, and they were quickly routed. A barricade of carts, furniture, and wooden barrels blocks the roadway at this point. The obstruction is draped with ribbons of fresh seaweed and the long-dead skeletons of the city’s defenders. Creatures: The first wave of pirates to press this far into the city inadvertently impaled themselves on the spears of the city’s defenders as they scrambled over the barricade. Exthenios left them where they died, but King Herrion’s curse has since reanimated them. As the PCs approach, the deathless pirates wrench the spears that killed them from their ribcages, then turn to attack the party. When Hermia the Wayfarer reached the barricade, she suspected the skeletal pirates might not rest soundly and chose to avoid the obstacle entirely. Her grappling hook is embedded at the top of a nearby building, still dangling a length of rope. Repository TITANBANE Chapter 1: In Search of a Blade Chapter 2: Shades of PolDhuraxilis Chapter 3: A Sleeping Titan Wakes Continuing the Campaign Kardaji Bay Adventure Toolbox Moderate 7 A short walk from the impromptu barricade (area A2), the PCs find themselves before the portico of a white marble building. The building’s ornate architecture sets it apart from the more austere structures in the city. Exthenios and his crew forced their way in when they arrived, but rusty iron hinges suggest a pair of heavy wooden doors once blocked the building’s entrance. The building’s interior is a cavernous space, with a long, marble counter spanning the entirety of the northern wall. To the south of the counter lie the rotting remains of desks and chairs, partitioned from each other by collapsing reed walls. A vault door ten feet across dominates the space behind the counter, a rusting metal dial set into the wall beside it. Angered by the recent construction of the island’s seawall, Gozreh sent a massive storm to sink the better portion of Pakilykos’s shipping fleet. The resulting lull in trade, combined with the exorbitant cost of rebuilding the fleet, forced the city to empty its coffers. When Exthenios and his crew landed on the island, much of the citizenry retreated to the repository. Sadly, the pirates overcame the building’s defenses and, disappointed by the paltry treasure to be found inside, locked the citizenry inside the near-empty vault to die a slow, extended death. Exthenios 18 This temple was a center of worship for Pakilykos before its fall, and the final stage for its tragedy. Though the chamber once held an altar to Gozreh before the city’s fall, enough citizens had converted to Herrion’s cult of Chinostes that the altar was replaced by a statue of Chinostes. This offense, along with the construction of the city’s seawall, enraged Gozreh and contributed (at least in part) to the city’s doom. When Exthenios mounted his raid against the island, many citizens fled to the temple of Chinostes to seek refuge in its inner sanctum. Unfortunately, the city’s militia was unable to rebuff Exthenios’s crew of trained murderers, and the temple was turned into a charnel house. Exthenios himself slew King Herrion, but with his dying breath, Herrion dragged himself to the foot of Chinostes’s statue to entreat his hero-god for justice. In far Reanpharos, Chinostes heard his supplicant’s call. He released a pulse of mythic energy to empower Herrion’s dying curse, dooming the soul of anyone who would steal the riches of Pakilykos to remain trapped on the island for all eternity. Herrion’s fateful curse struck down Exthenios and his crew in an instant, raising their corpses as undead. Creatures: At first, Exthenios reveled in the power that undeath brought him. The confidence to face any foe, the thrill of laughing off any blow! His joy turned quickly to rage, however, once he found himself unable to step foot aboard his ship to leave the island. Centuries spent trapped on Pakilykos have made the skeletal captain resentful, and even more malicious. Exthenios’s one respite from boredom came a decade ago, when Hermia the Wayfarer rose Pakilykos from the ocean’s depths. Though Hermia fought the captain bravely, Exthenios proved victorious, and in the aftermath of the battle, he claimed Hermia’s legendary weapon, Aerekostes. In the years since, Exthenios has regularly attempted to entreat Aerekostes, but the blade remains stubbornly silent. Though the pirate doesn’t understand the weapon’s true nature, he seeks to unlock the mythic power he senses flowing through it. At the moment, Exthenios believes that if he uses Aerekostes to shed the blood of a hero-god, the sword will find him worthy. When the PCs enter the inner sanctum, Exthenios challenges the most fearsome in arms among them to single combat. He leaves the rest of the characters to his minions, lashing out at anyone who interferes with his worthy duel. Though Aerekostes can’t free themselves from Exthenios’s clutches, they can nudge the odds in the party’s favor. Twice during the combat, when Exthenios achieves a critical success with a Strike using Aerekostes, the blade can turn the critical success into a success. The Hero Aerekostes Once freed from Exthenios’s grip, Aerekostes is more than willing to converse with the party. In a voice that rings like a tuning fork, the sword remarks: “What a relief to be in noble company again!” Aerekostes has remained silent since Hermia’s death, but not idle. Rather, they’ve spent their time reflecting on Pakilykos’s curse and observing the island for clues. Some questions the PCs might have for Aerekostes, as well as the sword’s answers, follow. How did you come to be wielded by these skeletons? “Hubris, mostly,” Aerekostes laments. “I had agreed to travel with a promising young hero-god named Hermia the Wayfarer. She was just coming into her own, you see, and needed to perform a heroic deed to meet her calling. She set her course to Pakilykos, and though I thought she might struggle to lift the island’s curse, I hoped to tip the scales in her favor. Sadly, both of us underestimated the strength of Herrion’s curse.” The blade’s tip sweeps toward a fresher corpse near the back of the temple: the body of Hermia. “Hermia fell, and I was taken as a prize.” Do you know how to lift the curse? “Hermia thought it was a simple matter of defeating these cursed pirates. Now I see we need to undo King Herrion’s magic at its source, here inside this temple.” Will lifting the curse prevent the island from sinking again? “I’m afraid not. The curse cast by King Herrion played only a part in Pakilykos’s fate. This temple was once devoted to Gozreh, and when Herrion cried out to Chinostes for salvation here, it was just one in a string of offenses against the god. In anger, Gozreh sent Pakilykos to the bottom of the sea. To keep the island above the waves, we’ll have to make amends to Gozreh.” We came here for you. Can’t we just leave now? “Perhaps, but Herrion’s curse is clear: those who seek to steal from the island can’t leave its shores. If you’ve looted anything from the ruins here, who knows 20 what might happen if you weigh anchor. And Hermia herself tried to break into the island’s vaults—against my advice, mind you! Though her bones remain still for now, I fear what might happen to her soul if we leave without breaking the curse.” Cleansing Pakilykos Unless the PCs have taken nothing from the island to this point, Aerekostes’s suspicion that King Herrion’s curse has affected them is confirmed the moment they try to leave Pakilykos. Any character who moves to return to the Tide Hunter finds their limbs gripped by a supernatural force that no amount of might or magic can break. The effect lasts only a few moments but returns as soon as the PCs attempt to leave the island again. Even abandoning or returning the looted items to where the PCs found them fails to break the curse. Of course, if the PCs haven’t taken anything, they’re free to leave Pakilykos at any time, though abandoning Hermia saddens Aerekostes, who believes they owe it to their former owner to complete the quest that brought them here. Assuming the PCs agree to Aerekostes’s plan, reversing the island’s fate requires two mythic deeds: breaking King Herrion’s curse and making amends to Gozreh by destroying Pakilykos’s seawall. Breaking the Curse Lifting King Herrion’s curse requires a simple, 10-minute ritual performed in the location the curse was first cast: the temple of Chinostes. At the end of the ritual, one character must attempt a DC 28 Arcana or Religion (trained) check. Other characters can Aid the check with Arcana, Nature, Occultism, or Religion. If the PCs freed the spirits trapped in the city’s repository (area A3), they might have learned a prayer to help put the spirits of the island to rest (“May we find the peace in death that was denied in life.”). Reciting the prayer grants the PCs a +2 circumstance bonus to checks made during the ritual. Similarly, if the PCs discovered King Herrion’s notes in area B2, the character leading the ritual gains a +2 item bonus to their check. Critical Success As success, and Chinostes grants each PC a blessing. As a free action when a PC would make a flat check to recover from bleed damage, that PC can utter a prayer to Chinostes. If they do, they automatically succeed on the flat check. Once a PC uses this blessing, the blessing on that character ends. Success King Herrion’s curse over the island is broken. The souls of Exthenios and his crew, as well as that of Hermia, are released to the Underworld. The PCs can freely return to the Tide Hunter at any time. Failure The ritual fails with no effect. Critical Failure The ritual backfires with disastrous results, siphoning the lifeforce of all the participants. The doomed value of any character who participated in the ritual increases by 1 for 1 week. If the PCs didn’t fully explore areas A or B and are struggling to complete the ritual, Aerekostes suggests that the repository or the king’s estate might hold clues that could help them. Similarly, if none of the characters are trained in Arcana or Religion, they can spend 1 Mythic Point to have Aerekostes make the check on their behalf, with a +13 bonus to the roll. Destroying the Seawall Once the PCs break King Herrion’s curse, they’re free to leave Pakilykos at any time. However, if they want to prevent the island from sinking back beneath the waves, they must make amends to Gozreh, the deity King Herrion offended when he converted the people of Pakilykos to Chinostes. While removing Gozreh’s altar from area C2 cemented the deity’s anger against the island, the true focus of their ire is the seawall King Herrion built to protect Pakilykos from sea storms. To make amends to Gozreh, the PCs must destroy the structure, but doing so is no mean feat: the project took several years to complete, and dismantling the seawall stone by stone would take a similar amount of effort. Aerekostes suggests the PCs walk the length of the seawall to see what might be done. A PC who inspects the island’s seawall can attempt a DC 28 Perception or a DC 25 Crafting or Engineering Lore check. On a success, the character notices a weak spot in the wall’s construction. Removing a single boulder in this spot would weaken the wall significantly, such that the entire structure would fail if struck by a powerful wave. To remove this keystone boulder, one PC must make a successful DC 28 Crafting or Engineering Lore or a DC 25 Athletics check. Among other methods of Aiding, a PC can use Gozreh’s lyres (either the one the party built or the one Hermia used to raise the island) to Aid this check using Performance. Once the boulder is removed, the PCs need only call upon Gozreh to send a wave against the island. Doing so requires a DC 28 Nature or Religion check. Once again, a PC can Aid on this check by making a Performance check to play Gozreh’s lyre. On a success, the air grows eerily still as the water level in Pakilykos’s harbor drops by several feet, as if the ocean were retreating from the island’s shores. Any character trained in Nature or Survival recognizes these signs as an indication that a wave of tremendous force is gathering, giving the PCs plenty of time to retreat to higher ground. (If the PCs fail to notice the signs, Aerekostes warns them instead.) Moments later, a wall of water several stories high appears on the horizon. On the deck of the Tide Hunter, Captain Yasmenei and her crew scramble to prepare for the approaching wave, but as the water rushes forward, it gathers itself into a shape like a giant’s fist. The fist strikes the weak point of the seawall, scattering the stacked boulders and causing the entire structure to collapse into the sea like a trail of dominoes. When the water recedes, the seawall is nowhere to be seen, but Pakilykos, the Tide Hunter, and the characters remain unharmed. Mythic Points: Exploring lost Pakilykos and returning to tell the tale is a mythic deed, as is breaking King Herrion’s curse and destroying the island’s seawall. Think on the matter, and I will do what I can to assist.” Kardaji Bay Adventure Toolbox 21 Chapter 2: Shades of Pol-Dhuraxilis Sangeh’s body lies beneath an island home to two Iblydan city-states: Pol-Dhuraxilis and Pol-Ungkore. Of the two cities, the heroes are most likely to find safe harbor in Dhuraxilis, as the residents of Ungkore are infamous for abducting and sacrificing hero-gods. What’s more, Aerekostes has an old friend living in Dhuraxilis: the prophet Iapholi, herself a local herogod. With the situation on Pakilykos resolved, the blade recommends that the party travel to Dhuraxilis to seek out Iapholi. While the PCs have been busy with their journeys to the Underworld and Pakilykos, the cult of Sangeh has not sat idle. Under the leadership of the stheno prophet Pteios, the cultists have thrown Dhuraxilis into political unrest, converting its oligarchs, propping up reckless hero-gods, and even sparking mythic 22 mutations among its citizens! The PCs soon find that Dhuraxilis is in desperate need of their help, and what was meant to be a quick stop turns into a fight for the future of the polis. About Dhuraxilis Ages ago, Pol-Dhuraxilis was much like any other city-state: a prosperous polity that clashed with rivals and exported sundry goods and livestock like timber, pigs, and weaponry. Its hero-gods were famous for their monster-slaying exploits as the expansive inland wilderness was the hunting ground for countless chimeras, griffons, giant serpents, and mythical beasts of all kinds. For generations, Pol-Dhuraxilis and its champions viewed these creatures as their adversaries. However, this perspective changed when Pol-Sylirica launched a massive invasion, its innumerable ships carrying legions to Dhuraxilis’s doorstep. The city-state might have fallen entirely had Dhuraxilis not received unlikely reinforcements: an army of monsters led by a daring harpy commander, Ekriathe. Together, they and Pol-Dhuraxilis’s defenders repelled the Syliricans and declared victory. In the aftermath, Pol-Dhuraxilis had to wrestle with its longheld prejudices, realizing that the creatures they had demonized—and not entirely without reason, given the chimera-burnt fields and citizens eaten by manticores— might be allies and even upstanding neighbors. Together, Ekriathe, her advisors, and the city-state’s council drafted new laws to both protect and police any monsters who wanted to live in Dhuraxilis. Ever since, Dhuraxilis has been a cosmopolitan port that welcomes any beasts who can follow basic laws, most of which involve protecting inhabitants’ well-being and property. Ekriathe attained hero-god status and has been reborn several times, with each incarnation manifesting mythic power and spell-granting abilities early in life. Most of these incarnations have overseen a generation of warfare and plunder, sating the bloodlust many monsters have suppressed to live in Dhuraxilis. The latest, a young woman named Iapholi, hasn’t raised the same bellicose banner, and many monstrous inhabitants grumble that she’s too peaceful. Kerinelopas 27 GENTLER MONSTERS Across the Inner Sea region—and throughout a large portion of Iblydos—Lamashtu is a deity regarded with hatred, disgust, and fear. Her role as the Mother of Monsters has given Lamashtu a well-deserved reputation as a goddess of slaughter and chaos, but like all things, there's nuance to her story. Though the founding of Pol-Dhuraxilis was bathed in blood, much of that violence was committed in the name of self-defense, as the killing of monsters (intelligent and peaceful or not) had become a cultural touchstone throughout the archipelago. Subtle societal shifts over the last 4,000 years have culminated in the rule of Iapholi, who fosters a fuller understanding of Lamashtu’s domains, some of which have been previously unexplored. The first of these concerns is care for the pregnant. Being always with child herself, Lamashtu understands the toll that creating life takes on the body. As a result, the citizens of Pol-Dhuraxilis do no harm to anyone who is pregnant or caring for a newborn, and the city offers free medical care to any expecting parent who requires it. Second is family. Many of Lamashtu’s creatures travel in packs for safety and strength. Similarly, the citizens of Pol-Dhuraxilis form close-knit bonds within their family units and any chosen family they acquire throughout their lives. While these family units often find themselves at odds with other families, it is rare for a citizen of PolDhuraxilis to betray or harm another member of their kinship group. Finally is acceptance of monstrosity. In other places, those born with the blessings of Lamashtu are often shunned, but in Pol-Dhuraxilis, such differences are celebrated. Acceptance of a person’s physical form also extends to “normal” humanoids who have been changed through magical or alchemical means, either accidentally, by force, or willingly through body modifications. These so-called monsters are not only treated as normal in the city, but lauded for their variations from the norm. Event 7: Undermine the Rivals The party has grown in experience since they sent their rivals packing earlier in the campaign, but that doesn’t mean the trio has hidden themselves away to lick their wounds. Since the PCs last saw them, their rivals have slain a nest of hydras, recovered treasure from the wreck of a divine pleasure barge, and accomplished other mythic deeds that have kept them apace with the heroes. When they arrived in PolDhuraxilis a few weeks ago, they adopted a new name of Akki's design: the Thunder Triumvirate Banner. Akki then immediately embarked upon a tour of the city’s taverns, boasting of the Triumvirate’s deeds until their legend caught Encymion’s many ears. At first, Encymion met with the Thunder Triumvirate Banner merely to determine how much truth there was to Akki’s tales. Once he concluded that these newcomers were, in fact, heroes of note, he began to consider how best to use them to unseat Iapholi. Since then, he’s seen the Thunder Triumvirate Banner quell an impending storm, repair city walls with a wave of the hand, and create alchemical wonders previously unknown to the polis. Encymion now truly regards the Triumvirate Banner as worthy replacements for Iapholi. He’s even discarded his waning faith in Lamashtu and pledged his devotion to these living gods. Bolstered by Encymion’s support, the party’s rivals strut about Dhuraxilis with little caution. After the disturbance in the marketplace (Event 4), the Triumvirate quickly hears about the party’s arrival, but they remain confident that their powers have exceeded those of the heroes by now. Tsemone elects to keep to herself, brewing new poisons from the comfort of her lab in Encymion’s compound. Meanwhile, Ulshuk spends his time in contemplation, praying to Nethys for guidance about how best to deploy his burgeoning mythic power. Only Akki can reliably be found out and about, as she spends most of the day regaling anyone who will listen with tales of the Thunder Triumvirate Banner’s achievements. If the PCs try to track down Akki, they quickly discover she isn’t hard to find; otherwise, the party stumbles upon Akki by chance. The meeting occurs on a crowded street, where the tengu woman is recounting the Thunder Triumvirate Banner’s latest adventure to a crowd of admiring citizens. Akki seems even more confident than she once did, moving with a swagger that can be gained only from too many easy successes. She carries a spear of polished bone, its metal blade hammered to give it the appearance of scales. Dangling from a leather cord around her neck is daggersized fang with veins of sickly yellow webbing dried across its surface. “Well, well, what have we here?” Akki says. “I remember you little ox-stains. Did you get taller? I was sure I could have kicked you clear across the polis.” She gives a playful wink to the assembled crowd. “Come to think of it, maybe I still can!” “Is this one of your old rivals?” Aerekostes thrums quietly. “She does seem the fool. And no better place to make that clear than a crowded street, eh?” Influence: Picking a fight with Akki will only result in the PCs looking like bullies to the onlookers; if the PCs don’t realize this themselves, Aerekostes advises that, while Dhuraxilis values strength, winning a battle of wits against their rival is more likely to get the citizens on their side. The battle of wits against Akki is an Influence encounter (Pathfinder GM Core 187), in which the PCs have 45 minutes (3 rounds) to embarrass Akki and turn public opinion against her. Each round, Akki makes a number of checks equal to one fewer than the number of PCs (so three checks, if you’re playing with a four-person party), accumulating her own pool of Influence Points. The influence stat block for the crowd follows. Akki’s statistics as of this adventure are on page 38. Mere hours after the ritual, he leaves Dhuraxilis to seek out Pteios, who’s in the wilds outside the city preparing his ritual to reawaken Sangeh. In the eyes of Pteios, Encymion’s machinations play no part in his scheme to rouse Sangeh from her slumber. The PCs can ask Iapholi additional questions, but beyond what’s she’s already told them, she has no idea what they might encounter in the chimera’s compound. Encymion’s Compound The varied citizens of Pol-Dhuraxilis require different types of structures for their living spaces. Flying creatures such as harpies construct towers lacking ground-level entrances or build nests atop more traditional buildings. Centaurs favor open spaces, with their districts more akin to parks. Meanwhile, minotaurs create maze-like neighborhoods, complete with covered walkways, twisting cul-de-sacs, and other architectural flourishes. Accustomed to the subterranean caves of his ancestors but also enjoying the company of flying beasts, Encymion opted to burrow his lair deep underground, then had a rookery constructed atop it. When he first met the Thunder Triumvirate Banner, Encymion invited the hero-gods to move into his compound, giving each of them their own space designed to suit their passions. When the PCs arrive at his compound, Encymion is elsewhere in the city preparing to challenge Iapholi during the March of Monsters. However, each member of the Thunder Triumvirate Banner is at home, ready for a final showdown with their old enemies. Unless otherwise noted, all areas of the compound are unlit. The ceilings of the chambers are 15 feet high, with 10-foot-high passageways connecting the areas. Use the maps on page 34 for these encounters. E1. The Rookery Moderate 8 Like many such structures in the city, Encymion’s tower 36 has no entrance at street level. The top of the tower is shaped like the basket of a torch, with a 10-foot-high wall pierced by balconies encircling the roof. Climbing to the top of the 80-foot-tall structure requires a successful DC 26 Athletics check. Alternatively, PCs can reach the top of the tower through magical means, such as the fly spell. The edges of the tower’s roof extend outward from the center, stretching over the streets below like the petals of a flower. A ten-foot-high wall rings the rooftop, broken only by a narrow balcony in each cardinal direction. A breeze from the bay blows through these openings to create a hollow whistle. Beyond the balconies, a shaft in the rooftop opens into the tower’s interior, though the area beneath it is lost to darkness. Creatures: Encymion allows a nest of griffons to occupy the roof of his home, feeding them scraps like a human would with stray cats. The griffons don’t take kindly to intrusions, attacking anyone who sets foot on the roof. Racks heavy with weights, discuses, javelins, and other sporting equipment line the walls. A shaft in the room’s ceiling extends upward, while double doors stands in the center of southern wall. Ulshuk’s Prayer Room This cavern is appointed with a simple sleeping mat and a writing desk crowded with stacks of books. Against the southeast wall sits a wooden shrine. Atop the shrine, a mask—one half made from onyx and the other from pearl— rests among a dozen or so candles, each carefully trimmed of rampant wax. Regardless, the space suits him well and now serves as a place of quiet contemplation with Nethys, the All-Seeing Eye. Treasure: Among the books on the desk are two lesser electricity breath potions. Development: A PC who succeeds at a DC 25 Perception check to Search the desk discovers a hidden drawer containing Ulshuk’s journal. The hero-god has taken to recording his thoughts about his personal journey toward his mythic calling, which he sees reaching its inevitable conclusion when he transcends his physical body and becomes a creature of pure magic. Ulshuk’s journal details the changes he’s noticed in himself, both physically and metaphysically, since gaining mythic power. He observes his increased hunger for magical secrets, along with a greater need to power his abilities with the life force of others. Ulshuk writes that this must be assent from Nethys that his course is true, though Akki and Tsemone seem dubious. Ulshuk dismisses his comrades’ concerns and surmises that the time for him to sever ties with the rest of the Thunder Triumvirate Banner is fast approaching. Perhaps more pertinent to the party’s current quest, the journal also details how Ulshuk worked with Encymion to summon the vengeful shade that attacked Iapholi during the Bathing of the Bloodstone ritual. The iruxi cleric remarks how the chimera seemed unconcerned about disrupting a ritual sacred to Lamashtu. If released to the public, this evidence would prove damning for Encymion, and more than justify Iapholi’s decision to bring him to justice. E4. Tsemone’s Laboratory Moderate 8 The stench of sulfur fills this L-shaped room, where a dozen or more worktables have been arranged in orderly rows. A variety of alembics, beakers, and other alchemical tools covers the tables. There’s a single door to the south, while double doors open into the room from the north. Hackles Lowered With Encymion and the Thunder Triumvirate Banner defeated, peace—or at least what passes for peace in Dhuraxilis—returns to the city. As if to celebrate the PCs’ victory, the Bloodstone Festival carries on through the night and into the next morning. At some point the following day, Iapholi again summons the PCs to her estate to thank them for their efforts. She mentions that she hasn’t forgotten her promise to give them a blessing of safe passage but explains it will take a few days to prepare the ritual. Aerekostes suggests the characters purchase supplies they might need for the journey while they wait. To help pay for these purchases, Iapholi gives the party 250 gp, as well as a pair of armbands of athleticism made of leather tooled with a motif of a manticore in flight. In the aftermath of Encymion’s defeat, his followers lose whatever standing they once held in the city, particularly if the PCs make their findings from Ulshuk’s journal public. Meanwhile, support for Iapholi solidifies, and all talk of deposing her and attacking other city-states evaporates. In the following days, Dhuraxilis seems to take a deep breath as the citizens return to their more stable, relatively normal, lives. Having lost his puppet within Dhuraxilis, Pteios orders his remaining cultists to retreat from the city. He resolves to take Dhuraxilis by force once Sangeh awakens, informing his contacts in Pol-Ungkore that a group of hero-gods is about to depart from the neighboring city. He then seals the entrance to Sangeh’s cradle by reinforcing the sleeping ritual on the Granite Ox that lies atop it (page 51). Finally, in preparation for the party’s arrival, the cult leader spins the titan’s dreaming memories into a gauntlet of deadly hazards. While their adventures in PolDhuraxilis are over for now, the PCs soon find the story of their mythic callings is not yet complete. TITANBANE Chapter 1: In Search of a Blade Chapter 2: Shades of PolDhuraxilis Chapter 3: A Sleeping Titan Wakes Continuing the Campaign Kardaji Bay Adventure Toolbox 41 Chapter 3: A Sleeping Titan Wakes With a titan-finding weapon in hand and a blessing from a grateful city secured, the hero-gods must now face the ancient power behind their mythic callings: Sangeh, the slumbering titan of artistry. When Gorum and Gozreh defeated Sangeh eons ago, one of her most beloved creations, a titanic creature called the Granite Ox, laid itself across her fallen body to contain her leaking energy until she could recover. Critically wounded but not quite dead, Sangeh slipped into a coma-like slumber. Centuries passed before the island where Sangeh fell was discovered and settled by mortals—enough time for the earth to cover the forms of both the slumbering titan and the Granite Ox. Her body hidden safely miles below the ground, Sangeh’s psyche wandered, seeding Iblydos with inspiration, creativity, and just a hint of mythic power. 42 Over the countless years since, no artist, author, or thespian on Iblydos’s myriad isles has remained untouched by Sangeh’s influence. The various muses of each of these creatives have been, in truth, the titan’s slumbering essence observing their work and, at times, nudging them toward greater creative heights. Even Sangeh herself was barely aware of her influence— at least until Gorum’s recent death began to stir her from slumber. Having now recovered a measure of her former power, Sangeh’s memories of the vast history she’s observed have begun to form in her mind: an age’s worth of dreams she’s not yet awake enough to process. Pteios has attempted to converse with Sangeh since she first began to stir, and he’s formed his own ideas about what the titan plans to do once she awakens. Through a series of rituals that are now almost complete, Pteios intends to shock Sangeh awake and follow her as she unmakes the world, returning Golarion to both physical and metaphysical anarchy. Comfortably secure in the impact crater he’s dubbed Sangeh’s Cradle, the self-appointed prophet is committed to his course—and only a party of true hero-gods can stop him! Marching Inland This chapter begins outside the gates of Pol-Dhuraxilis, a few days after the conclusion of Chapter 2. Iapholi has outfitted the PCs with enough provisions for a 10day journey, as well as a rough map of the island’s interior. In addition, she’s performed a blessing of passage, which she assures the PCs will dissuade the island’s more aggressive inhabitants from bothering them as they make the trek to Sangeh. As the characters prepare to depart, Iapholi warns the party that several nearby villages friendly to Dhuraxilis have gone silent in the past few weeks. Iapholi assumed the settlements had fallen victim to raiders from Pol-Ungkore, but with the recent revelation that Sangeh has begun to stir, she now fears she was wrong. She makes clear that unless a resolution to the titan’s awakening can be found, a few missing villages will be only the beginning of Iblydos’s troubles. While this warning doesn’t lock the characters into a strict timeline, they should move with a sense of urgency, nonetheless. The gates of Dhuraxilis stand some forty feet in height, tall enough to accommodate nearly any creature that might come to call. The wooden gates are reinforced with bands of iron and carved with images of humanoids and monstrous creatures alike. Beyond the gates, the city’s paved thoroughfare transforms into a bare dirt road that winds along a stand of trees before disappearing beyond the horizon. Aerekostes rattles in their sheath. “Be cautious, my young heroes. I haven’t visited these woods since I still had flesh—the mosquitos were quite fond of it, as I recall. Maybe it will be more pleasant this time around?” The sword makes a low, thrumming sound. “But likely not. It was inhospitable then, and it’s likely worse now that Sangeh seems set on upending the Universe. She seldom makes improvements, does she? Perhaps we should ask her about that point. Believing that this surge of mythic power could create new hero-gods, the cyclops Iristelos journeyed to the area to study the phenomenon. Unfortunately, Iristelos’s sensitivity to mythic energy exposed him to an overwhelming number of Sangeh’s memories. Now convinced that tapping into Sangeh’s dreams will return the gift of prophecy to the cyclopean people, the seer wanders the forest in search of anything—or anyone—imbued with mythic power. The party encounters Iristelos a few hours after setting out from Stone Pit. The sound of the massive cyclops stomping through the forest is hard to miss, and as they approach, Iristelos mutters to themself 47 about “seeing with sight” and “prophecies of the mother.” If the PCs seem to expect a battle, Aerekostes urges restraint, advising that whoever approaches could be touched by Sangeh’s power. “They might be able to give us a lead,” the weapon says. “If they prove amenable to talking.” Initially, Iristelos treats the party as a curiosity, looking each character up and down and referring to them by their mythic callings instead of by name (“You there, Caretaker! What balm do you possess to soothe the titan’s wounds?”). Iristelos begins the encounter as indifferent, but the PCs can improve their attitude by indulging them in various tests of mythic power. For each of the PCs, devise a short mythic trial they must complete to impress Iristelos. The trials should be tailored to the characters’ abilities and mythic callings, they shouldn’t require more than three skill checks each to complete, and they should allow a PC to fail at least one check without ending the challenge prematurely. Challenges might also provide minor boons or treasures. Examples of such trials follow: • Acrobat’s Calling: The PC must succeed at an obstacle course that comprises three challenges. The first challenge requires a successful DC 28 Acrobatics check or DC 30 Athletics check. The second requires a successful DC 28 Athletics check or DC 30 Acrobatics check. The final challenge requires a DC 30 Acrobatics or Athletics check. The obstacles involve mundane challenges that must be handled in an atypical way (such as climbing a tree without using one’s arms) as well as foreboding challenges that involve no restrictions (such as swimming up a waterfall). • Bookkeeper’s Calling: Iristelos challenges the PC to a trivia contest, with subjects drawn from multiple disciplines. The PC must succeed at three DC 28 checks to Recall Knowledge on at least two different subjects. • Demagogue’s Calling: The cyclops studies the PC for a moment, sensing some ethically dubious action they took earlier in this Adventure Path. He then debates the PC about the act’s morality and justification, taking whatever stance the PC doesn’t. The PC must succeed at a DC 27 check, a DC 29 check, and finally a DC 31 check to debate, using skills such as Deception, Diplomacy, Intimidation, or Performance (though other skills might apply). • Guardian’s Calling: Iristelos challenges the PC to earn the blessing of Queen Kaiphere, an ancient tyrant of Pol-Ungkore who boasted so loudly of her countless servants that the hero- 48 gods transformed her into an immortal termite queen. Her hive is only a short walk away, but getting answers isn’t as simple as casting speak with animals and asking nicely. The PC must disturb the nest and shrug off her servants’ bites until at last the queen must admit defeat, emerge, and speak with the PC; she understands and can raspily speak Iblydosi. Doing so involves taking 4d6 piercing damage and 4d6 poison damage three rounds in a row (DC 29 basic Fortitude save for each). If the PC critically fails a saving throw, the pain is so great that they instinctively flee the nest and must start over. The PC earns the queen’s blessing so long as they withstand the termites and speak with her. If the PC critically succeeds at one or more of the saving throws, Queen Kaiphere praises the PC’s resilience and shares additional wisdom to resist the attacks of many, granting that PC resistance 3 to the attacks of swarms and troops until the end of this adventure. • Hunter’s Calling: The PC must make two successful DC 31 Survival checks to Track the flight of a passing manticore. The PC doesn’t need to defeat the manticore in combat, only follow the creature to its lair. • Thespian’s Calling: Iristelos challenges the PC to recite a poem so moving that the trees themselves weep. The PC must succeed at three successful DC 29 Performance checks. If they succeed, nearby trees release a fraction of their leaves as if autumn had arrived early. If they critically succeed at a check, sap begins running down the trunk of one tree like tears. This sap can be collected and bottled, functioning as a moderate elixir of life. • Thief’s Calling: Iristelos dares the character to painlessly pluck a pegasus’s flight feather, noting that the feathers of local pegasi discolor shortly after being shed naturally or extracted violently. Iristelos gives the PC directions to a nearby roost where pegasi gather. The PC can extract a feather by approaching without frightening the pegasi, be that with a DC 29 Deception, Diplomacy, or Stealth check. The PC can then Steal a feather (a closely guarded object) surreptitiously with a DC 31 Thievery check. Failing the Thievery check likely results in the pegasi angrily stampeding, chasing away the would-be thief with a torrent of sharp hooves. Creatures: Iristelos has too much to learn from Sangeh’s dreams and no patience for those who waste their time. If the party fails at two or more of their trials, the seeker flies into a rage and attacks. Event 14: The Granite Ox Extreme 9 The Granite Ox was one of Sangeh’s final creations before the gods struck her down. The assembled diplomats fade away, leaving Pteios and the PCs alone together in the council room. The stheno slaps his stone fist into his other palm in a slow clap. “Well argued,” he says wryly. “I can see how you’ve made it this far. Let us see what else you can do.” With that, the vision fades, and the PCs find themselves back in the crater. Judging from the water level at the bottom of the crater, several hours have passed. “We should hurry on before our titan is completely submerged,” Aerekostes offers. Reward: Grant the party 10 XP for each Influence Point they earn during the debate, to a maximum of 60 XP if they earn 6 Influence Points or more. G3. The Battle of Lovrediemos    Moderate 9 Outsiders have long considered the city-state of Pol-Sylirica to be the pinnacle of Iblydan military might. Proudly bearing the epithet “Sylirica of Seven Armies,” the polis observes a longstanding warrior tradition, where soldier is the only worthwhile career and all others exist solely to prop it up. Because the minds of Sylirica’s citizens are ever set on expansion, many other nations have needed to rebuff incursions from the city. Scholars with a firm grasp of Iblydan history, however, know that Pol-Sylirica is hardly unstoppable; most of the city’s campaigns have failed. A famous example is the Battle of Lovrediemos, when the army of Pol-Liachora lured Sylirican forces into a deadly trap. Confident in their superior numbers, Sylirica marched into a fetid bog, where the Liachorans had the advantage of terrain and maneuverability. Led by their hero-god Vastillinos, the Liachoran troops carved out a narrow victory against the Syliricans, in what otherwise surely should have been a rout. Though not her favorite form of artistry, Sangeh nonetheless regards tactical ingenuity as a form of creativity. She watched the Liachoran victory with interest and has developed a particular fondness for the battle. The memory comes to her as she watches the PCs—now battle-hardened hero-gods in their own right—reach the bottom of the crater and begin their journey to its center. The water at the bottom of the crater has pooled to a depth of about two feet. Banks of thick fog move about the landscape, and as one of them passes, the scenery changes once again. The crater is now filled with crooked trees, their low-hanging branches sagging to brush the waterline. The smell of peat fills the air, and all about, the sound of drums and soldiers marching through muck can be heard. Suddenly, the figure of a lean dromaar general appears atop a nearby hummock. He wears an ancient breastplate etched with the heraldry of an eye floating between the crests of two waves. The dromaar begins to speak, addressing a crowd that can’t be seen. “Brave citizens of Liachora!” the general calls. “The Sylirican warmongers have taken our bait. Here, in the mire of Lovrediemos, we will prove that their seven armies are made of nothing but bullies and fools.” He raises his spear, and moments later a host of ethereal soldiers appears before him, beating their weapons against their shields in response. “For the City of Tides, and the lives within them!” Characters that succeed a DC 26 Society or DC 24 Heraldry or Warfare Lore check can identify the details of this memory: namely, that Pol-Liachora prepares to battle the invading forces of Sylirica in the bog of Lovrediemos. Aerekostes comments that they grew up on stories of this battle and can’t wait to see it play out in person. Creatures: Sangeh’s memory of the Sylirican troops is of a disciplined fighting force that employed a shield wall to ward off missile fire while using pikes to repel melee combatants. This formation was nigh-unbreakable if maintained perfectly, but it quickly fell apart when disrupted. As Vastillinos, the dromaar general, leads his troops against the spirit warriors of Sylirica, the PCs must battle a phalanx of soldiers that—for the moment at least—are all too real. The water at the bottom of the crater mimics the actual conditions of the battle of Lovrediemos, wherein the agile Liachorans proved more mobile and adaptable than the rigid Syliricans. The water here has pooled to a depth of several feet, causing all spaces to become difficult terrain. The Titan of Art Extreme 10 The journey from the battle of Lovrediemos to Sangeh’s resting place is a mile-long slog through increasingly deep water. Luckily, after only a few minutes, the PCs spot a beacon of blue light rising from the center of the crater: a spiritual manifestation of the titan Sangeh’s mythic power. By using the beacon as a guide, the PCs can easily find its source. When they do, read or paraphrase the following. 59 The source of the blue beacon is a hundred-foot-tall sapphire rotating slowly above the crater’s floor. Within the gemstone, a shape of equally titanic size can be seen. The figure wears a flowing chiffon gown splashed with paints of all colors, and her skin is marked with a swath of scar tissue from neck to hip. Below the sapphire stand the ruins of some ancient structure, now sinking beneath the rapidly rising waters. The sapphire radiates a palpable heat that causes the water beneath it to spit and boil angrily. “Here we are, I suppose,” Aerekostes whispers in their sheath. “I will surprise no one and confirm that this indeed is Sangeh. The question now is what to do.” “What to do indeed, my well-struck hero-god,” replies a voice from within the sapphire. “I only ask that before you act, weigh carefully the consequences of your choices—and pray speak with me a moment as I begin to reawaken.” Though Pteios has not yet completed his ritual to reawaken Sangeh fully, she is conscious enough to speak with the party from inside her sapphire cocoon. She can’t move or affect anything outside the sapphire, but she’s quite interested in knowing what the group intends for her. She listens patiently as the characters introduce themselves, remarking that she’s watched their actions during her unconscious wandering. “I am Sangeh, once known as the titan of the arts. Rather than submit to the permanence the gods chose for the world, I wished to keep it ever-changing, as dictated by my imagination. For that crime, the god of war struck me down. I know now that Gorum has met his own doom—in battle I hope, as he no doubt would have wished. “I presume you’re here to finish Gorum’s task and kill me. But if all you seek is safety for your world, that might not be needed. I realize now that the stability the gods craved failed to halt all change, as I once feared it would. Perhaps—” The rest of Sangeh’s words are cut off as a second figure materializes atop one of the walls beneath the titan. The stheno wears a green tunic with bright gold accents and a leather harness holding multiple javelins across his back. His left arm is made of black stone from elbow to fist; the PCs can easily identify the man as Pteios, Sangeh’s self-proclaimed prophet. Two living statues carved with the same eerily lifelike features as the petrified sthenos of Stone Pit appear in the water below him. With a level voice that barely conceals his contempt, Pteios addresses the party. 60 “I’m impressed that you have made it this far,” the man begins. “I am Pteios, prophet of Sangeh, the titan of art and imagination, who is the source of your powers. We’ve never met, but you’ve hounded my steps for some time.” The man turns to face the floating sapphire. “My lady,” he says. “Please allow me to speak with these interlopers and test their intentions for you.” With that, the stheno waves his working hand toward the gemstone. As he does, the light within the sapphire dims, and Sangeh’s figure slumps as if asleep. Creatures: Pteios was fetching materials for the final ritual to free Sangeh when the party arrived. Though he has no intention of leaving the titan’s fate up to the PCs, he’s open to a debate of ideals before initiating combat. If the party obtained Eylthia’s blood in Event 11 (and didn’t use it to cure the residents of Stone Pit), they can offer the vial to the stheno by attempting a DC 29 Diplomacy check. On a success, Pteios is tempted enough by the offer that his self-doubt makes him stupefied 1 for the first round of combat (or stupefied 2 on a critical success). In any case, Pteios eventually ends the conversation, announcing that he refuses to be swayed by the party’s rhetoric as he orders his living statues forward to attack. During the battle with the PCs, Pteios casts spells and uses his Petrifying Gaze mythic ability from his perch atop the ruined wall. Meanwhile, the living statues protect him, Grabbing the characters to prevent them from escaping the boiling water. Regardless of whether Pteios lives, Sangeh addresses the party again, asking what the hero-gods intend to do with her. The titan admits that she hasn’t been in control of her powers to this point. Now that she’s nearly awakened, however, she’s able to process the thousands of years of history her wandering spirit has observed. “I’ve learned,” Sangeh says, “that stability does not mean stagnation. Despite what Pteios thought, imagination and art can flourish without the need to unravel reality.” A hint of a smile crosses the titan’s face. “At least not entirely. If you allow me to awaken, I promise to reign in my powers, sparing Iblydos from the chaos it has seen in recent months.” Sangeh’s offer presents the party with a few choices. If the PCs are unsure of their options, Aerekostes establishes the stakes. • Kill Sangeh: As foretold, Aerekostes has the power to end the titan’s life, though the weapon points out that doing so will cost Iblydos its font of mythic power, forever ending the birth of new hero-gods on the archipelago. If the PCs choose this course, Sangeh willingly accepts her fate, agreeing to sacrifice her life if it means saving Iblydos. To kill the titan, the PCs need only touch the tip of Aerekostes’s blade to Sangeh’s sapphire prison. Doing so causes the gemstone to shatter spectacularly into a thousand pieces. No sign of Sangeh’s body can be found among the shards. • Subdue Sangeh: If the PCs choose not to kill Sangeh but feel uncomfortable simply letting her roam free, they can put her back to sleep. Aerekostes confirms that they can lead the party in this ritual, but doing so requires that the PCs sacrifice their mythic potential, rendering them “mundane” heroes. Sangeh doesn’t object to this plan. “My sleep was pleasant,” she says. “I wouldn’t hate to return to it.” Putting Sangeh back to sleep quells (but does not quench entirely) the surge of mythic energy sparked by Sangeh’s awakening. In the following days, life in Iblydos returns to status quo. • Befriend Sangeh: If the characters release Sangeh as Pteios intended, Sangeh can roam the archipelago as another living goddess. In this case, Sangeh assures the hero-gods that once she regains control of her powers, she will exercise restraint, reducing her output of mythic energy to a trickle: enough to birth new hero-gods, but not so much as to put Iblydos in danger. TITANBANE Chapter 1: In Search of a Blade Chapter 2: Shades of PolDhuraxilis Chapter 3: A Sleeping Titan Wakes Continuing the Campaign Kardaji Bay Adventure Toolbox Concluding the Adventure No matter what fate the PCs decide for Sangeh, their choice has ramifications not just for themselves, but for all of Iblydos. By preventing Pteios from recklessly unshackling the titan of art, they’ve fulfilled their mythic callings and become true herogods of Iblydos. As the characters return to the Tide Hunter and continue their adventures, word of their deeds spreads throughout the archipelago, and their cult continues to swell with new adherents. What the PCs do next is in part determined by how they choose to deal with Sangeh. While every group’s campaign is bound to be different, you can get ideas for where to take the story next in the Continuing the Campaign section on page 62. 61 62 Continuing the Campaign With the conclusion of the Myth-Speakers Adventure Path, the PCs have accomplished something truly legendary as they accepted and explored their mythic callings. Yet even greater triumphs and challenges await such heroes in the future as they progress into their mythic destiny. Mythic callings conclude their journey at 10th-level and mythic destinies begin to have their impact at 12th-level, meaning that mythic characters have time to prepare for their ascension into their mythic destinies. This can translate into a bespoke adventure created by you to bridge the storylines between their mythic calling and mythic destinies, or you could opt instead to run a published adventure or scenario here. Legends to Explore If you and your group wish to continue with the PCs of Myth-Speakers without leaving the lands of Iblydos, this gives you, the GM, a great opportunity to craft a custom campaign for your players to enjoy. Many challenges fit for PCs building upon their mythic destinies exist in and around Iblydos. Presented below are several legends and myths that you can use as inspirations for your own games as you continue the campaign. After this, additional player options for exploring mythic destinies in Iblydos are presented. (Note that if your group is continuing on into Revenge of the Runelords, though, that Adventure Path has its own thematic options for mythic destinies that should be used instead!) The Behemoth Ousmariku From the desk of Psomeira, Divine General of Aelyosos, Hero-God of Seasons and Spears—a note that the PCs might come across on a dead messenger who was on his way to ask for aid: “We approach the annual time for tribute once more, with hope that the terror below will pass over Aelyosos once more and not swallow it like it did our sister city-state of Liachora. Each year, the tribute grows. This year, the seers say that we must feed it the wheat harvest—all of it. Perhaps it is time to slay it by pretending to feed it a hero-god, only to have it slain from within. “Pros: The beast will be dealt with for once and all. “The chosen can retrieve the tribute from the years past, and the treasures of Aelyosos and Liachora returned to us. “We will not starve. “Cons: The chosen may die and strengthen the behemoth with their power. “Pharimia, lady of ports and who worries over all the hero-gods, will seek to prevent the plot. “If we fail, the behemoth will swallow us in anger.” Ongalte’s Return The hero-god Ongalte did her own myth-speaking at the collapsed temple at Hoimpeia. She herself died in that attack but rose from its ruins a day later, whereupon she carved a bloody swath through the land with her axe. If the PCs wish to discover what caused her return from death and resultant killing spree, the best place to start is by studying her victims. Victims 1–3: Her first three victims were murdered in a killing spree before her ascension was known. One of the victims is the Golden Spire, hero-god of heights and temples. The Golden Spire was already gaining power when she was killed, while the other two victims are unknown. Identifying these victims will assist in answering a greater question: what does she receive from each death? (Attempted) Victim 4: Failed attempt at killing her defected lieutenant, Ytildos. He likely has information on her favored tactics. Victim 5: Body left mangled and attached to the mast of a shipwreck. Difficulty approaching due to chimeras nesting nearby. Recommend retrieval of body. Appears to be attached with an arrow, most likely dawnsilver. Consider retrieving for use in scrying. They did not know that the lamb’s mother was the dinner of a lion, and the lamb was to be dinner for the lion’s cub. With its child’s meal taken from it and not replaced, the lion’s stomach turned to poison out of anger. It stalked the hero-god as they ate their supper, and then it leapt! However, the hero-god was clever and dug their dagger into the lion’s stomach. 63 The lion slunk away, dagger still in its flesh and weeping poison from the wound in its viscera. The poison burns away at anything it touches, blighting any living thing. That dagger can kill anything it touches, but retrieving it means killing the lion whose anger has made it immortal. Perhaps it is time for a hero-god to go to the Island of Poisoned Wrath and feed the long-starved cub. Perhaps the right hero-god can kill that which refuses to die. Bound in Chain When the great beast of Pol-Ptirmeios was bound in chains and sealed away, the hero-god of bindings and promises hurled the key as far as they could. They flew great distances, only to land in the crook of the tree. Over time, the branches grew around the key. No marking identifies the tree, except that any who eat its fruit find themselves bound to any promise that they speak. The beast stays bound, never able to be an ally when the city falls into danger, never able to be fully destroyed so the citizens can sleep soundly in their beds. No, to free it requires finding the tree, tearing out its roots as they dig into the ground, and retrieving the key from its very heart. Even then, with the key found to unlock its great collar, a beast bound so long will not welcome its rescuers. Granite Ox Island When the PCs awoke and rode the great Granite Ox slumbering atop Sangeh’s sanctuary, the beast bolted into the shallow sea before settling back down for a lengthy snooze. The new island quickly attracts a mix of wildlife, as well as entrepreneurs hoping to use the unique promontory as a hideaway or fortress for controlling nearby traffic. The Granite Ox will likely Granite Ox Island 64 sleep through most of these visitors’ antics, yet it’s only a matter of time before someone identifies the rare minerals that speckle the beast’s body, sets up an ill-advised mining operation, and risks awakening the titanic creature. Revenge of the Runelords In the Revenge of the Runelords Adventure Path, a group of mythic heroes must rally to oppose the return of one of Golarion’s most infamous and dangerous threats. Spoilers for that campaign are kept light here, but there is one thing you’ll want to decide if this is the route you and your players wish to take: how do heroes from Iblydos make their way across the world to the Saga Lands, and why are they the heroes who are destined to stand against the runelords’ revenge? The Revenge of the Runelords Player’s Guide (a free PDF downloadable at paizo.com once this new campaign launches) will provide some context to your players, but as the GM, you should take this opportunity to make some behind-the-scenes decisions on how you’d like to tie Myth-Speakers in to Revenge of the Runelords. One potential option is summarized below. The Revenge of the Runelords Player’s Guide begins with the PCs experiencing a powerful shared dream in which a potential ally and an unknown enemy make contact. In this dream, it is revealed that these PCs are the ones destined to stand against the coming perils threatening the Saga Lands, and in that dream they face their first mythic challenge as those who have chosen their destinies. In the first adventure of Revenge of the Runelords, this dream takes place on the night before the adventure actually begins in the capital city of New Thassilon; the PCs have already traveled here to take part in a festival meant to celebrate the activation of a trade portal intended to link the remote capital to the city of Absalom, and thus to usher in a new era of prosperity between New Thassilon and lands far beyond its remote borders. If you intend to run Revenge of the Runelords next, there are two ways you can transition into this story. First, Queen Sorshen, ruler of New Thassilon, invites a wide number of heroes and notables to her city to take part in these celebrations. While the heroes of Myth-Speaker are located some distance away from the Saga Lands, the impact they’ve had on Iblydos and the world at large is not something that Queen Sorshen, one of the most powerful wizards on Golarion, would fail to take note of. Her invitation to attend the festival should come to the PCs well in advance, so that they’ll have time to make the journey from Iblydos across continents and oceans to the shadow of Mhar Massif, where her capital city of XinEurythnia (once known as Xin-Shalast) awaits. This journey should not be without its challenges, as the PCs must step in to deal with potent threats along the way—threats that should reward them with enough XP to reach 12th level just as they reach Xin-Eurythnia and have their eerie shared dream. Alternatively, this shared dream could take place not long after the PCs complete the current adventure. As presented at the start of Revenge of the Runelords, this dream presents a challenge that uses the chase rules, as the PCs outrun a series of progressively dangerous apocalyptic visions in their dream. In this option, though, you can expand that chase out into a series of encounters that take place in an immense dreamscape. Rather than have the PCs resolve each section as a mere chase obstacle, they must do so in encounter mode, facing increasingly dangerous fights and hazards and earning XP (and treasure, of course, that remains with them when they awaken) along the way. When they awaken from their dream, they find they’ve traveled across the world while they slept, and have awoken in the high mountain city of Xin-Eurythnia. With this opening, you’ll need to adjust the party’s arrival in the city— but perhaps the same shared dream they had was also experienced by certain others in Xin-Eurythnia, such as the priestess of Nocticula‚ Ayavah, who welcomes these new heroes into the festival. Hero-Gods of Iblydos The hero-gods of Iblydos dwindle in numbers. The city-states of the archipelago remain structured around their local hero-gods. Each death increases the panic that Iblydos will tip into a new era, one of a cultural legacy that cannot be accessed by modern society. The hope that prophecies may be restored and the city-states rise again strains against this nearly certain future. Those who receive a promise of greatness from the cyclopean myth-speakers find power waiting for them—both the power granted by their mystic destiny, and the power of a culture hoping they will restore Iblydos’s lost fortune. To become a hero-god of Iblydos, a PC must first complete a legendary quest on the isles of Iblydos and establish themselves as someone worthy of worship to the people of the land. In the Myth-Speaker Adventure Path, all of the PCs automatically qualify for this requirement as soon as they complete the campaign— their encounter with the titan Sangeh and their actions in that event are precisely the sort of deed from which hero-gods are born. It’s not until you unlock your mythic destiny, though, that you officially become a hero-god. While NPC hero-gods can be custom built as the GM desires, all PC hero-gods are mythic characters who have chosen the Godling Dedication (War of Immortals, pages 130– 133). While a hero-god can progress along this destiny simply using the options presented in that section, the following three additional feats are available for herogods to select as their mythic destiny feats. HEROIC WEAKNESS FEAT 14 RARE MYTHIC Prerequisites Godling Dedication, hero-god accomplishment As word of your faith spreads, so too does word of your foibles and weaknesses. Where originally these disadvantages may have been myths themselves, or simply manifestations of ill fortune or chance, when you take this feat, one of those weaknesses becomes real. Work with your GM to choose your heroic weakness—it must be to a specific damage type and must be associated with a specific condition, both of which must be elements that are going to be significant parts of your story’s future. For example, you could choose for a weakness to be spirit damage caused to you by a follower of a rival god, physical damage from a specific category of weapon, void damage caused by a specific kind of undead, or fire damage taken in a certain part of the world or from creatures from that part of the world. The amount of weakness you gain to this damage is equal to twice your level. But with this new weakness comes a new source of power, for when your foes would take advantage of your weakness, you can use the pain and humiliation to bolster your own resolve. You gain the following reaction. Makes Me Stronger [reaction] Trigger You take damage from your heroic weakness and are not reduced to fewer than 1 Hit Point by the damage; Effect You make a show of powering through your weakness, be it by flexing your muscles, issuing a challenging roar, laughing off the pain, or simply acting as if the damage doesn’t worry you in the slightest. Your spells gain a status bonus to damage against the triggering creature equal to twice their rank; this lasts until the next time you use this reaction. In addition, the creature that damaged you with your heroic weakness must attempt a Will save against your class or spellcasting DC, whichever is higher, to avoid becoming frightened 1 (frightened 2 on a critical failure). Your myth includes amusing parables of clever plans and sly maneuvers, often applied to small things in life such as disguising yourself as a sheep to ambush a wolf or tricking a snake into shedding its skin. MYTH OF REALM-WALKING FEAT 14 RARE MYTHIC Prerequisites Godling Dedication, hero-god accomplishment Your myth speaks of distant travel to countless countries, planes, or dimensions.
