If it was already broken, it is destroyed. 69 70 Kardaji Bay TITANBANE Chapter 1: In Search of a Blade Great and ancient Iblydos rises from the midst of Kardaji Bay, a region of ancient kingdoms, broken empires, and independent spirit that is now part of the vast Padishah Empire of Kelesh. The bay’s glimmering ports count among the wealthiest in all of Casmaron, and while imperial rule keeps an enduring peace, old rivalries linger still, and the tumultuous developments of the Godsrain and the War of Immortals have cast the region in a looming sense of uncertainty. New divinities emerge from the muck of prehistory, beckoning their followers toward rebellion. Tragedies in Kelesh’s royal family and the ascendance of disreputable leaders in the heartland further weakens their grip on the region, and as the throne grasps tighter to protect its power, the resentment of the folk of Kardaji Bay grows deeper, and local affairs push ever closer toward chaos. A map of Kardaji Bay appears on the inside front cover of this book. The Deep Well of History Long before the dawn of recorded history, the earliest human settlers of Kardaji Bay were explorers of the ancient empire of Khattib. Extending north and west from the lush jungles of the southern arm of the bay, the Khattibi strung a series of settlements along the northern coast of the bay, pulled along by the lure of trade with the burgeoning cultures of ancient Avistan. In time, these settlements formed the basis for the trade route that would become known as the Golden Road, a conduit of commerce that remains strong to the present day. In time, the powerful northern nation of Ninshabur swelled to an empire that ranged from Iobaria southward along the inland Castrovin Sea and across the trackless central deserts to Kardaji Bay. The armies of Great Ninshabur scattered and absorbed the coastal settlements, pushing Khattibi political influence back to the jungles from which it had emerged and establishing a series of coastal cities even more resplendent than those of the imperial heartland. In the vast mountainous plateau looming over the forested plains north of Khattib, Ninshabur established deep and bountiful copper and tin mines, forming the colony of Hukaris to administer them and ensure that their wealth made it safely back home to Ninshabur. Many centuries later, this realm was among the first on Golarion to master the secret of iron, and the land between Hukaris and Kardaji Bay became known as the Iron Coast. Later, in the Age of Legend, the seafaring Aishmayar culture of the island of Iblydos took advantage of widespread chaos in Ninshabur to lay siege to the coastal cities of Kardaji Bay, sacking their great ziggurat temples and claiming their ruins as their own. Over a series of long decades, the Aishmayar managed to displace the Ninshaburians, isolating Hukaris and the Iron Coast and dominating the northern coast with newly established palace-cities of their own in the regions known today as Midea, Mishyria, and Qadira. Centuries of political and military struggles between the Aishmayar cities and their rivals along the Iron Coast, Hukaris, and Khattib ensued, bathing the region in blood and conflict and generating countless cultural heroes, godlings, and legends that underscore local folklore even still. The tragedy of Earthfall devastated Casmaron, casting most of the old empires into abject ruin. Forewarned of the disaster by their precognitive cyclops allies, the people of Iblydos weathered the cataclysm better than most, establishing a second generation of colonies along the north coast. Shielded from the worst by luck and geography, the realms of Hukaris, Khattib, and the Iron Coast similarly gasped back to life during the Age of Darkness. But Darkness gave way to Anguish, and in –3923 AR, the Pit of Gormuz opened in the ruins of Ninshabur, disgorging the great beetle Ulunat, first of the Spawn of Rovagug. Hordes of refugees fled in all directions but particularly to the coastal settlements of Kardaji Bay, collapsing the region’s delicate infrastructure and rendering it ripe for conquest by a new regional power—Althameri warlords from the central deserts near Ayyarad—the progenitors of what would become the Padishah Empire of Kelesh. In roughly a century, the vast armies of Kelesh conquered the last of the Aishmayar cities of Kardaji Bay. Throughout the Age of Destiny, the empire expanded its dominion to include all the nations of the region, including Khattib, Hukaris, and the Iron Coast, a confederation that persisted throughout Chapter 2: Shades of PolDhuraxilis Chapter 3: A Sleeping Titan Wakes Continuing the Campaign Kardaji Bay Adventure Toolbox 71 the whole of the Age of Enthronement and into the present. The recent War of Immortals has once again cast the region into chaos, rocking the politics and stability of Kelesh and sparking new impulses toward freedom and rebellion in its vassals in the region, nearly all of whom once harbored imperial ambitions—and glittering realities—of their own. Perhaps the cleansing waters of the Godsrain have given these old empires a new opportunity to be born once more. Regional Faiths The early Ninshaburian settlers of Kardaji Bay brought with them a vast pantheon of gods that for the most part was made up of deities present during the imprisonment of Rovagug under Gormuz during the Age of Creation. These divine beings—particularly Sarenrae—took personal interest in the affairs of their devoted adherents, manifesting among them in physical form with a frequency that would astound a modern denizen of Golarion, even in the immediate aftermath of the recent War of Immortals. Although Earthfall brought a swift end to nearly all direct deific influence in the region, several of these “Ninshaburian” gods maintain strong followings to this day. Thus do the folk of Kardaji Bay still honor the likes of Abadar (often called Abdur), Desna, Calistria (known locally as Kellis), Pharasma, and the like. Gorum, the Lord in Iron, was particularly popular in Hukaris and along the Iron Coast, and his death has thrown at least three major holdings among the Unbroken League into chaos. Today, Sarenrae is the chief divinity of the Padishah Empire of Kelesh, and most citizens of the modern empire consider any deity worshipped in its lands Keleshite, no matter what cultures it may have been associated with in the past. This extends as well to otherworldly entities of the Great Beyond such as the archdevil Moloch and empyreal lady Falayna, whom most locals consider of similar renown to an Iblydan hero-god. Deities of cultures absorbed by Kelesh, such as the Khattibi commerce goddess Destho and her cousin Oathos the Ever-Lost, likewise find their way into a common regional pantheon, their adherents spreading from their original lands to every corner of the empire. Some regional gods, such as the ancient Hukarian storm god Umarik, his brilliant wife Anras, and their countless children, remain fiercely independent, their cults showing little interest in being appropriated into some common Keleshite cultural association or absorbed into an unfamiliar pantheon. Even more resistant to outside control is the newly reborn goddess Etaris, who emerged during the War of Immortals to remind the once-proud folk of Mishyria of their own past glories long before the arrival of Kelesh. Even though ages have passed since Etaris, the “Bride of Ydersius,” descended into the underworld to steal cultural, magical, and technological secrets from the serpentfolk, Etaris’s message resonates with many: independence from an uncaring empire is the only path toward greatness and restoring Mishyrian identity. This revived faith increasingly clashes with Sarenrae worship. More information about Etaris appears on pages 96–97 of War of Immortals. Hukaris Drawn to the region’s dense deposits of copper and tin, Great Ninshabur settled the realm of Hukaris as a mining colony early in the Age of Legends. Anvil-priests of Gorum unlocked the secret of iron smelting, vastly improving Ninshabur’s weaponcraft and military might. After Ninshabur withdrew from the region, hardy mountain folk from Hukaris surged westward and conquered the coast, eventually establishing a small empire of their own. In time, their conquered territory became known as the Iron Coast, a region that exported iron across the sea and established trade with covetous markets as distant as Osirion and Kaladay. Eventually, Khattib took advantage of internal tumult within Hukaris to claim the southern city-states of the Iron Coast, but Hukaris itself never fell to Khattib, and remained independent (if increasingly starved and decadent) until their much later absorption as a dependency of the Padishah Empire of Kelesh. Even today, some of the best swords in Casmaron come from Hukarian anvils. Weapons and warcraft have held Hukaris in their grip since the earliest days, and while Kelesh eventually brought the realm into its empire thousands of years ago, Hukaris maintains a fiercely independent spirit backed up by an aggressive culture well steeped in violence and battle. The trio of dour, cone-crowned sovereigns who rule Hukaris— the so-called Forge-Kings of Zurakan—consider themselves more akin to battle allies of Kelesh than subjects of it. They send soldiers to aid in the empire’s defense when required, provide opulent tribute to the emperor every year, and (of course) pay their taxes on time and by the shipload. In matters of domestic policy, they behave as their forebears have for countless centuries—as brutal tyrants. The Forge-Kings rule from the walled city of Zurakan, at the foot of the famous Mount Jabel, where the great Hukarian storm god Umarik, his consort Anras, and their family of local deities are said to have dwelled since the region’s original Ninshaburian gods left with the Ninshaburians aeons ago. These local gods are associated with the region’s original Qalah people, and hearken to the spirit of independence that three empires—Ninshabur, Khattib, and Kelesh—have failed to break. From its lofty perch in the high mountains, Hukaris leers down at the Iron Coast, coveting city-states it once held under its thumb, biding time as the empire seems poised on the edge of crisis. The decrepit Emperor Kalish XXII is on his deathbed. Queen Shubat lacks the love of the people, and trusts her wicked son Yaril, who seems the likely heir when all is said and done. Like the lions that serve as the nation’s symbol, Hukaris waits for the moment to strike. Khattib Fueled by trade with Vudra across the Betul Sea and bolstered by an almost impossibly diverse array of natural resources spawned in its dense primeval jungles, Khattib is among the most prized jewels in Kelesh’s imperial diadem. The same wealth that funds its famous libraries and impressive architectural masterpieces draws raiders from the mountains to the north (notably bestial humanoids, giants, and unruly brigands escaping the harsh punishment of Hukaris), as well as pirates from the Unbroken League to the north or rogue states of Vudra. Khattib is famous across Casmaron for its staggering stone temple-cities, each a reflection of the nation’s wealth and devotion to its numerous deities. Midean humans are generally short with ruddy complexions and dark hair, being an admixture of Ninshaburian, Aishmayar, and Keleshite ethnicities. They are known for their elegance and love for fine things, especially rare sea creatures dredged up from the bay, which Mideans devour with enthusiasm. Fauns thrive in the wild lands near the mountains that divide Midea from the central deserts of the imperial heartland, and minotaurs predominate in the mountain foothills. Minotaurs once held a more significant role in Midean culture—many of the nation’s finest stone monuments and structures were built by their hand—but the horned folk came under scrutiny and eventual persecution in the first decades of the Age of 75 Enthronement, when the rebellious minotaur warlord Voradni Voon led an army of centaurs out of the Grass Sea and destroyed three Midean cities. Of Midea’s major settlements, only Kalios, the capital, escaped some measure of destruction. Following the ambitious minotaur lord’s defeat by Aroden on the Isle of Kortos in 23 ar, Kelesh established the new nation of Thieron from the northern half of the Iron Coast as a sort of safe harbor for those minotaurs who did not swear fealty to Voon, and many of Midea’s more “civilized” minotaurs abandoned Midea. Those who remain tend toward secluded lives in cave communities and seldom venture into the cities many citizens still blame them for destroying nearly five thousand years later. Midea’s current governor, Chelis, counts among the closest friends and confidantes of the noblewoman Layilah al-Parishat, niece to Kelesh’s queen and the preferred “sane choice” for the permanent successor to the badly ailing and deeply ancient Emperor Kalish XXII. Sadly, Layilah vanished during a military action in the Grass Sea following the Godsrain, and today Chelis finds herself politically isolated, shunned by the increasingly powerful prince Yaril, who seems poised to inherit the empire. Relations with Thieron are stronger than ever, but chaos to the west in Mishyria puts Midea in a delicate position, and Chelis is not the only Midean who fears for the future. Mishyria Mishyria formed the heartland of the Aishmayar conquest of the north Kardaji coast in ancient times, and has persisted in one form or another for thousands of years. Unlike its cousins Qadira to the west and Midea to the east, who have generally thrived due to deep harbors and close access to foreign markets, Mishyria’s historical glory came from the conquests of its armies. For millennia, Mishyrians made up the bulk of Aishmayar and colonial Iblydan armies, resulting in a highly regimented society and militaristic traditions that persist to the present day. Recruits from Mishyria traditionally compose a significant portion of the empire’s elite fighting forces, making the boar-tusk helms common to its military a symbol of Keleshite dominance and regional strength. For countless generations, the irrigated coastal Plain of Anvar provided a huge measure of the empire’s food, particularly dates and pomegranates that boast a reputation for deliciousness that spans eastward past Vudra and westward as far as Cheliax. Ever since the dawn of the Age of Enthronement, however, Mishyria has suffered a series of tragedies and natural disasters unparalleled in the region, making the lands between Midea and Qadira dangerous and 76 unpredictable. The greatest of these catastrophes was surely the destruction of Mishyria’s cities at the claws of the terrible beast Urarkuun, a lesser Spawn of Rovagug disgorged from the Pit of Gormuz about a thousand years ago. The powerful armies of Kelesh could do nothing as the enormous winged beast devoured Mishyrians by the thousands and crushed its great works into oblivion. For centuries, the empire watched in horror as Mishyria fell into banditry, its finely trained soldiers devolving into disciplined raiders who effectively cut off Qadira from the empire. With nothing left to lose, many Mishyrians swore an oath of to the archdevil Moloch in exchange for protection and support, becoming the Beshzen—the People of the Pact—harbingers of a new era for Mishyria. For three centuries the Beshzen ruled Mishyria, reestablishing its ruined cities and bringing a dark and terrible order to the ravaged nation. Loyal Mishyrians, backed by Kelesh, implored the heavens for assistance. This drew the personal attention of the empyreal lord Falayna, who personally fought against the Beshzens and reclaimed the cities of Misyhria, casting the devil worshippers into the northern mountains. During the recent War of Immortals, storm clouds heavy with silver Godsrain converged over the reservoir above Mishyria’s ancient Daszij Damworks, pouring down for seven days until the dam collapsed, flooding the Plain of Anvar and recalling the devastation of ancient days that had put Mishyria on a tragic path. The drained reservoir revealed an ancient temple complex dedicated to the old Aishmayar goddess Etaris, who emerged in physical form from her time-lost tomb to chart a new and glorious future for the people of Mishyria. Though Falayna and her followers immediately swore fealty to the old goddess made flesh, the imperial court of Kelesh remains far more circumspect, and fears that Mishyria is once again slipping from the dominion of the empire. Thieron Historically, the northern half of the Iron Coast had stronger ties to Great Ninshabur and Hukaris than to Midea or Khattib, even if the whole of the coast served as the primary battleground between the latter two empires. Especially in the north, proximity to the societies of Iblydos and Midea (and later conquest by Kelesh) resulted in a highly diverse society rich in cultural and religious syncretism, and the realm’s eventual absorption into the Padishah Empire of Kelesh continued this status quo. And while Thieron boasts people of all ancestries populous in the region, the nation is particularly sacred to minotaurs. The initial subjugation of Midea by Kelesh saw minotaurs harshly persecuted and their religion repressed in a series of atrocities that were ultimately responsible for the rise of the rebellious minotaur warlord Voradni Voon in the first decades of the Age of Enthronement. After Voon destroyed several of their cities, Midea established Thieron as a safe harbor for those minotaurs who remained loyal to the empire. The minotaurs who settled there also made Thieron the center of their cultic worship, which focuses on the sacred Brother Bulls, Belech and Cormion (their horns said to be locked in an eternal contest for dominance). Today, Kelesh rules more through financial conquest and political guile than outright tyranny. Generally speaking, the minotaurs and other inhabitants of Thieron get along with their imperial governors and consider themselves citizens of Kelesh as much as citizens of a nation with a proud independent history. Still, pockets of open resistance remain, especially as the countless census-takers loyal to the wicked Prince Yaril scour the land for citizens infused with deific power from the Godsrain during the War of Immortals, scooping up a disproportionate number of local nephilim and other gifted individuals. Rumors of a reborn Voradni Voon somewhere in Avistan are igniting impassioned hearts with the fire of nationalism and independence, a development looked upon in the imperial court of Kelesh with a sense of abject dread. Throughout Thieron, great stone works of minotaurs, both ancient and modern, draw visitors and pilgrims from all around Casmaron. The famous sunken churches dedicated to the Brother Bulls are particularly noteworthy, often carved from the bedrock itself and connected to vast tunnel complexes with deep religious significance to many of the region’s powerful mystery cults and oracles. When Keleshite armies invaded Thieron, many minotaurs seemingly abandoned these sites, though in fact they had sought refuge in (and periodically launched guerrilla raids from) dozens of hidden entrances and settlements scattered deep underground. No doubt many of these ruins are waiting to be rediscovered by adventurers. Most notable among these works of monumental architecture is the cliffside temple complex known as Tokanos, where the immortal medusa oracle Ilegia augurs the future for a procession of blindfolded initiates that often includes powerful regional politicians and nobles, merchant princes, and prophets. Her words carry power—power that unscrupulous visitors are tempted to buy to ensure she delivers politically useful proclamations. That said, her sanctuary is decorated with statues of those who sought her cooperation through excessive flattery and bribes. The Unbroken League In ancient times, the petty kingdoms, isolated citystates, cultic enclaves, and warlords of the Iron Coast ranging from the Bull’s Head to below Hanzar’s Blade served as the primary battleground between the cruel forge-kings of Hukaris and the warring empires of Midea and Khattib. These greater powers generally subjugated the smaller kingdoms here, playing off their vassals against one another to prevent any potential pretender from gaining the support needed to challenge their hegemony. This approach kept “independent” rulers in power but stunted the formation of a united identity for the subjugated kingdoms beyond that of their controlling empire. Following Earthfall, the dozen or so shattered client states here became engrossed in internal competition for resources, favoring their own survival over the dominion of greater powers who had pressing problems of their own. This reality has persisted more or less to the present day. The region was the last of the Iron Coast to fall under the control of Kelesh. When defeat finally came, it did so in the form of a fairly generous series of concessions guaranteeing political semi-independence and freedom from military incursions in exchange for regular tribute in the form of treasure, specially crafted weapons (the region’s traditional mastery of iron has in modern times extended to the production of high-quality steel goods), and conscripts for the vast armies of the emperor. The resulting Unbroken League is united on paper only, with each kingdom maintaining fierce independence and often clinging to centuries-old grudges. In fact, Kelesh has long relied on this competition; the more that the League fights among itself, the less they combine forces or challenge the Padishah Empire’s ongoing hegemony. Twelve autonomous holdings comprise the Unbroken League. The most influential is Ketarkus, realm of the influential death cult known as the Dark Passage. Situated along the River Damophan where it curls around the great holy mountain Yatanu, the robed cultists control the Terminus Gate, an ancient entrance to the Darklands (which many in the region consider a portal to the literal Underworld where souls linger after death). Other notable holdings in the League include Heshaga, seat of the immortal ooze-lord Gellix; the Plains of Xexos, realm of a great centaur tribe called the Eudoxos; and the old city-state Arazak, whose sovereigns claim to have killed three foreign emperors in ancient days. The whole of the Iron Coast is a hotbed of intrigue and scheming, and much of that effort has been directed toward Kelesh. After generations, the people of the Iron Coast seek freedom. The presence of an enormous, one-eyed giant can be quite alarming, and others’ panic is not conducive toward quiet study or long-term research. Accordingly, these cyclops seekers often develop methods of changing their shape to fit in more easily among the societies they wish to learn from. Some cyclopes pursue knowledge, power, and artifacts from a bygone era—particularly those recovered from regions where ancient cyclops nations once stood. These cyclops seekers hone their brief insights into epiphanic bursts of inspiration to better uncover forgotten truths. A rare few become philosophers and sages, whether as secluded hermits or as gregarious guides eager to share the wonders they’ve discovered. These talents are more common among the introspective cyclopes of Iblydos. Cyclops seekers are particularly fond of collecting scrolls, grimoires, and other objects of magical lore—even accidentally foregoing rest and meals when devouring esoteric textbooks, historical documents, and fiction. Those with a good sense of humor realize the irony of trading their physical hunger for their eternal thirst for knowledge, though failure to achieve a breakthrough can lead a cyclops to ruminate, becoming sullen and withdrawn. When they’re too large to safely study an interesting set of more compact ruins, a cyclops seeker might hire on smaller adventurers as reconnaissance teams or research assistants, but woe to those who doublecross their scholarly employers, for while the cyclops seeker is a studious creature, they’re also deadly in battle. Chapter 1: In Search of a Blade Chapter 2: Shades of PolDhuraxilis Chapter 3: A Sleeping Titan Wakes Continuing the Campaign Kardaji Bay Adventure Toolbox 83 Leviathan Louse EXTERMINATING LICE As part of their invasion of the Plane of Metal, denizens of the Plane of Earth attempted to weaponize leviathan lice to simply eat the enemy’s fortifications. This didn’t endear them to the inhabitants of the Plane of Metal. Removed from their normal environments and deliberately starved, the leviathan lice devastated both architecture and local populations with their insatiable appetite for iron. Farmers, miners, and jewelers see little practical distinction between leviathan lice and their waterwalking ore lice cousins, moving to eradicate any they see on sight. Particularly enormous and ancient creatures from the Plane of Earth often find difficulty keeping their bodies mobile; over time, slow-growing crystals glue limbs together, gravel clogs the joints, and countless other maladies gradually inhibit their already limited flexibility. While good hygiene can help, these routines can be unfeasible for particularly massive entities who spend much of their lives inert, in hibernation, or far from an ideal mountain to itch against. Enter the strange and unsettling leviathan louse. These stone-hungry creatures resemble their smaller, more mundane cousins with bumpy, iridescent exoskeletons, but they’re individually the size of a horse. Colonies of leviathan lice form symbiotic relationships with massive, rocky earth elementals, feeding on their rocky barnacles and (often literal) veins of minerals, in exchange for keeping their host clean. While they have little interest in feeding upon creatures closer to their own size, leviathan lice are quick to defend their territory, biting enemy combatants with massive mandibles or swiping with spiny forelegs. Rarely does a louse stray far from its host or find its way to planets like Golarion, but left to its own devices, it can reduce a rich mine to a crumbling, empty cavern in a matter of weeks. An adult leviathan louse is about 9 feet long and weighs between 1,500 and 2,100 pounds, though larger specimens raised on a plentiful, supernatural diet of strange ores or stone do exist. An adult lays eggs in crevices in the host’s exterior. The larvae grow slowly, molting at least six times before reaching adulthood after several decades. These cast-off molts occasionally contain trace amounts of valuable metal that an industrious prospector might recover. It has an automatic result of 42 on Deception checks and DCs to pass as a mural. 87 Iapholi Child of the Bloodstone In the early days of Iblydan culture and earliest generations of myth-spoken hero-gods, Iblydos was home to an even greater concentration of bizarre beasts and terrifying monsters. Most of these early hero-gods earned their power by slaying these entities, building their legends on the corpses of hydras, griffons, and even intelligent species such as sthenos and minotaurs. This continued for an age, until the fearsome beasts were all extinct or chased to the wilderness, rarely daring to approach the growing city-states. Though relegated to the periphery, these creatures nevertheless called Iblydos home. Thus, when an army from Pol-Sylirica invaded its southern neighbor, PolDhuraxilis, an army of monsters led by the harpy Ekriathe emerged from the latter’s forests and hills to help fight off the intruders. Though shocked by the unexpected assistance—and raised to view monsters with mistrust—the people of Dhuraxilis were thankful. In the aftermath, the government overhauled its laws, and its people wrestled with their prejudices, resulting in a city-state that welcomed and represented monsters. For her leadership, Ekriathe received every honor, including a myth-speaking that led to her ascension to hero-god status. In the millennia since, Ekriathe has been reborn numerous times in different bodies, her different incarnations often separated by many generations. The cult of Ekriathe Revivalism watches for and raises these rare reincarnations, known as Children of the Bloodstone. After centuries without, in 4202 ar Pol-Dhuraxilis at last welcomed Ekriathe’s seventh incarnation, a nephilim named Iapholi. As is tradition for Ekriathe’s successors, Iapholi is a representative of and champion for monsters across Iblydos. The nephilim Iapholi was named Child of the Bloodstone by the Revivalists as an infant in 4202 ar, assessing the Mother of Monsters’ favor based both on Iapholi’s eclectic animal features as well as myriad omens that accompanied her birth. She began presiding over rituals and ceremonies by age 6 and began issuing decrees of her own design by age 10. Under her stewardship, Pol-Dhuraxilis has gained not only peace, but respect among other city-states, 88 rising above the base assumption of it being a chaotic hovel of monsters. Her efforts to maintain stability and growth without bloodshed might have impressed the outside world, but they’ve rankled the more aggressive oligarchs in Dhuraxilis. After all, they reason, Ekriathe’s successors are supposed to herald an age of monstrous strength, ferocity, raiding, and Lamashtufueled revelry. Yet this incarnation promotes peaceful confidence and coexistence! Many question whether the Ekriathe Revivalists interpreted the omens correctly, hinting perhaps that Iapholi isn’t Ekriathe’s successor at all. Even so, enough citizens believe in Iapholi and her policies that the bitter traditionalists lack the strength to revolt. Iapholi is far from helpless, despite having peaceful hopes. In 4221 ar, she led a vicious defense of Dhuraxilis’s exterior settlements against a bold incursion from Pol-Ungkore’s bounty hunters. Believing the polis easy pickings for a source of rare creatures, an ambitious mercenary outfit raided nearby farms and killed a couple families of centaurs in the process. Iapholi responded by raining curses down upon them from the back of a mythic griffon while Dhuraxilis’s militia of terrifying creatures ran through the camp. Iapholi sent back the heads and other choice remains to Pol-Ungkore as a warning. The polis later passed a ban on hunting within a twenty mile radius of Dhuaxilis’s territory, which has been strictly enforced by both cities. The events of the Godsrain and Sangeh’s shifts within her deep slumber have robbed Iapholi of the trust her previous victories once afforded her. When world-shaking events leave their scars on Golarion, the incumbent powers often look weak in response. Pulses of mythic energy have hit Dhuraxilis hard, given its proximity to the titan and the already volatile nature of its inhabitants. Mutations gone awry have led to small riots and unsolved murders— most of which would have felt almost normal a decade ago before Iapholi stabilized the city. Seizing this opportunity to disrupt her leadership are powerhungry groups such as Encymion’s hardliners and the Rivals. Without some dedicated outside help, stewardship of Dhuraxilis will fall into bloodier hands, renewing it as a den of monsters that strike out at the other cities in the region and paint the coast red. Campaign Role Aerekostes leads the party to Iapholi’s door to seek help in narrowing down the location of Sangeh, somewhere deep in the mountains of the island that houses Dhuraxilis. While Iapholi is more than willing to help, she’s in a protracted political struggle for control of her city and cannot offer significant aid at first. As the party explores the city-state’s ongoing events, they help Iapholi, subsequently freeing up her resources and allowing her to act more boldly. She gathers leads on the sleeping titan and useful supplies for their journey inland. Though the continued rule of Iapholi is integral to the stability of Kardaji Bay, the more immediate concern for the party is to not lose their best ally in the city. If Dhuraxilis falls to the likes of Encymion, the hero-gods will be moving inland with a growing force of riled up monsters at their backs, leaving no safe place to retreat if their journey goes awry. While more withdrawn and prone to dreaming than the rest of the hatchlings, there was no real sign of the turn his life would take. When he reached adolescence, fate played its hand—an errant gaze at his hand from another young stheno caused his fingers to become stone. The community’s elders were at a loss, for sthenos had always been exempt from the calcifying eyes of their peers. Worried that Pteios might be vulnerable to further petrification, the community sheltered and later relocated him to be raised abroad by a friendly foster family. This, however, proved to be unhelpful. In addition to leaving him jaded and resentful, the petrification gradually migrated from his hand up along his arm, sapping much of the limb’s flexibility. With a display of grim calculus, Pteios kept his hand grasped to hold utensils for two years as it turned to stone, maintaining some use of it even after it became fully immobile. He labored where he could to buy a spellcaster’s services to reverse the petrification, yet this only alleviated and slowed the transformation. The dread that he would one day become one of the statues he had grown so fond of carving ate at his soul. His frustration at his inescapable reality finally became so great that he retreated to a tiny island off the coast of Pol-Bailax, seeking a peaceful place to become a statue. But the Universe had other plans. As he rested, the chaos that would be remembered as the War of Immortals erupted across the multiverse, and fragments of the shattered war god Gorum fell as the Godsrain across reality. One of these crashed into Pteios’s island. Curious, he stiffly hiked over to the smoldering crater and reached out with his petrified hand to nudge the otherworldly fragment. As he did, a torrent of visions coursed through him mind. He could sense the distant battles among the gods, a thousand wars fought across Golarion, the roar of armies fueled by Gorum’s bloodlust, and the dying gasp of the Lord in Iron. At last, a relieved voice in his head concluded “He is dead!” But who was it? Again, scenes played out across Pteios’s consciousness, showing Gorum and Gozreh chasing a titan who seemed to be made from 90 living paint. The two gods cornered her over coastal waters before Gorum delivered a terrible blow. As the two gods departed and the titan’s body sank into the water, the seafloor rose to cocoon her in the islands of what would one day become Iblydos. Amazed, Pteios beseeched the voice, asking what he could do to help. He received only faint and vague answers—a name, a direction, and a hope to beautify the world—as if the entity were drifting in and out of sleep. As he became aware of his surroundings once more, Pteios realized he hadn’t just contacted a forgotten divinity; his body was entirely healed of the petrifying affliction! Grateful and filled with zeal, Pteios retrieved the fragment of Gorum and set out to evangelize the forgotten titan and healer, Sangeh. Wielding a spear shaped from the Gorum fragment, Pteios has performed tiny miracles as he travels across Iblydos. At each island, he recruits downtrodden followers and tries to sense Sangeh’s location again, gradually triangulating where her body is entombed. He has taken a special interest in Pol-Ungkore and Pol-Dhuraxilis. In the former, his mythically empowered gaze petrified many of the city-state’s ruling council, sparking a civil war that’s only recently begun to die down. In the latter, he has leveraged his own monstrous appearance to recruit followers—even if doing so challenges the influence of Pol-Dhuraxilis’s own hero-god, Iapholi. Most recently, Pteios discovered where his patron resides, buried in an underground city trapped beneath a mountain. With Sangeh’s blessing, Pteios has managed to part the stone, descend to commune directly with her, and encourage her to awaken as swiftly as possible. The titan shares countless memories with him in the meantime, and her prophet studies these with great interest, like a thespian soaking in a stage play. By the time the new hero-gods set out on their adventure, Pteios has laid much of the groundwork to wake Sangeh. The titan begins to stir on her own, and the stheno has accumulated enough mythic power in the furtherance of his calling that he believes he can give her the final jolt. All that’s left is to ensure Pol‑Dhuraxilis is unstable enough to welcome its new patron deity with open arms. Campaign Role Pteios serves as the primary antagonist for the MythSpeaker Adventure Path, though the details of his identity remain obscured for much of the adventure. He’s only passingly aware of the party’s efforts to stop Sangeh from waking, but he becomes more interested as they draw ever closer. By the time the group reaches PolDhuraxilis, the prophet decides to take a more active hand in the city’s fall and lends Encymion resources to that end directly. When the chimera’s assassination attempts fail, Pteios retreats fully to Sangeh’s cradle and prepares his ritual to wake her. If Pol-Dhuraxilis is not ready for a willing occupation by the worshippers of the titan, he reasons, it will have to fall by force. Uncertain if he has the power to combat multiple hero-gods at once, he barricades the entrance and pulls memories from Sangeh’s dreams to buy time. Ever curious about views not his own, Pteios is willing to converse with the party during their final encounter. Those who do find him to be a quick-witted philosopher, if one who greatly fears a death not of his choosing. It’s not possible to sway him from his course or convince a surrender, but Pteios will grimly admit he would have enjoyed a different outcome before engaging in combat.
